# Copper demand growth – Is the answer blowin’ in the wind? There has been strong growth in renewable power capacity installations over the past few years, driven by attractive financial incentives and an increased consciousness of environmental awareness. Wind power has taken a good share of this expansion. In Western Europe, the focus for this _Insight,_ Wood Mackenzie estimates that installed capacity of wind power has doubled over the past five years. This Copper Market Service _Insight_ is investigating wind power given its potential impact on the copper market. We estimate that turbines on average contain 3.6 tonnes of copper per megawatt. Wind capacity installations are forecast to rise by 12% per annum over the next few years and despite its relatively small beginnings, this is an expanding market for copper, relative to stagnation in overall European demand. This _Insight_ reviews the current status of wind power generation, quantifies the use of copper in this sector and forecasts future prospects. Copper in wind power ## Wind of change Over the past decade the gradual increase in environmental consciousness, in addition to raised awareness that alternative sources of power are needed to sustain electricity demand has resulted in strong growth in renewable energy. In fact, according to the European Wind Energy Association (EWEA), of all power capacity installations in the European Union in 2011, 70% of these were renewable and 21% of the total was wind power. Renewable energy is rapidly increasing its share of total installed capacity, albeit from a low base. This is significant for copper because wind power is said to be three times more copper intensive than traditional power generation. The broad reasons behind this growth have been mentioned above but European Union member states are obliged to grow the contribution of renewables to the energy mix, while legislators have become cognisant of the political capital to be gained from being “green”. However, there are also sound economic and geopolitical arguments for investment in renewable energy sources. Surging fossil fuel prices over the past few years have prompted energy companies to look for less costly alternatives, while national governments are increasingly keen to move away from nuclear power generation. There has also been legislative pressure stemming from the European Union such as the 2009 EU Renewable Energy Directive, which establishes mandatory national targets with the aim of the achieving 20% of energy from renewable sources by 2020. ### **Cumulative wind capacity in Western Europe* - (MW)** 90,000 20

The combination of these factors has resulted in investment in renewable energy being incentivised in order to promote its growth.  Although these vary by country, incentives are largely centred on a system of feed-in tariffs.  They are typically paid to the renewable generator (usually by the transmission system operator) at a predetermined level instead of the generator selling their power to the market – the transmission system operator is then responsible for selling that power in the market to cover costs.  As a result, Western European wind power installed capacity has almost doubled over the past five years, rising from 41,064MW in 2006 to 81,338MW by the end of 2011.  Germany has a 35% share of this, with Spain (28%) the next largest market, followed by France (10%), Italy (9%) and the UK (9%).  Unsurprisingly, the pioneering countries in wind power of Germany and Spain are the largest in our data set.  Denmark is also one of the countries which was at the forefront of wind capacity installations, although is not included in our data. 

Initially growth was driven by on-shore wind installations although there has been a slight shift over the past few years with off-shore installations increasing at a sharper rate than overall wind capacity.  We estimate that of total capacity in Western Europe, less than 5% is off-shore, although around 9% of installations in 2011 were off-shore.  Part of the reason for this move off-shore is because locations that are suited to wind turbines are constrained by geographic features and the number of suitable sites is becoming exhausted.  In fact, some of the recent growth in Germany, for example, is as a result of replacing old turbines with larger more efficient ones.  Although costs are higher, off-shore projects also offer higher wind speeds and, potentially, the prospect of placing projects closer to demand centres as with the London Array project that we discuss below.  Meanwhile, local residents are increasingly objecting to wind farms near their homes and as such, these factors have combined to encourage turbines to be moved off-shore, where there are fewer constraints.

## In a world of magnets and miracles 

In a typical wind turbine, rotating blades (rotor) connect to a main shaft and gear box to a generator, which is connected to a transformer at the base of the tower.  The nacelle, at the top of the tower, houses the generator and gear box.  The tower is then linked to the grid via a sub-station and/or switchgear.  The basic principle of the turbine is that rotation of the blades powers the generator, which then converts kinetic wind energy into electricity. 

While we have conducted our own primary research, we have also compared our findings with data from the European Copper Institute, which was found to be broa

dly in line. Copper is used in significant quantities in the generator, the transformer and in general cabling, in addition to earthing or grounding equipment against lightning strikes. On average, on a per megawatt basis 0.7-4 tonnes are used in the generator, 0.85 tonnes in the transformer, 1 tonne in general cabling and a further half a tonne in earthing against lightning strikes and in miscellaneous uses. Clearly, there is a large variance in the amount of copper used in the generator and this is down to the use of technology. Without going into too much detail and simplifying things a little, there are two main types of technology; those with a gearbox and those without. A gearbox is used to increase the revolutions per minute from the rotor blades to the generator and this technology tends to use less copper because of the smaller number of electromagnets used. In gearless or direct drive Metals Market Service Insight - May 2012 Page 3 of 5 Copper in wind power turbines, the rotor is attached directly to the generator, but a larger diameter rotor is used to compensate for this. Because of the larger size, more magnets are required and this increases the use of copper. Overall, we have calculated a weighted average for copper consumed in turbines of 3.6 tonnes per MW, equating to some 200km of wire. A typical wind turbine Close up of nacelle

Significantly, our research only considers copper used within the turbines themselves, without consideration for the broader implications of the expansion of wind power. Clearly there is a requirement to connect wind capacity to the grid, and depending on the size of the farm this may be done through a sub-station on site, however, if there are only a few turbines or there is a sub-station nearby there might be no need for a dedicated sub-station. From this point there is a further requirement to connect to the power grid, although this is likely to be in the form of overhead conductor wire, which will certainly be aluminium and not copper. Even so, we believe that there could be as much as a further 50% more copper used in wind farm power interconnection cables and electrical distribution systems in addition to the turbine itself for on-shore installations. For off-shore wind farms, however, the situation is slightly different. Each wind farm will certainly have its own dedicated sub-station from where it will then need to reach land, which will almost exclusively be done through sub-sea copper cables. As such, the overall copper intensity or demand stemming from equivalent size wind turbines or farms is significantly higher for off-shore developments relative to those built on-shore. Indeed, in the example we illustrate below, four times more copper is used in related infrastructure

compared to the turbines themselves.  This is particularly significant because future growth in off-shore installations in Europe is likely to be at a faster rate than those on-shore. 

## Surfing in a hurricane – The London Array case study 

Currently in construction, London Array is set to be the largest off-shore wind farm to date, with over 1GW of capacity by the time all phases are complete.  Set in the Thames Estuary between Essex and Kent in the UK, phase 1 of this project will use 175 3.6MW turbines to give an overall capacity of 630MW, which should be able to power up to 450,000 homes according to the developer.  Over 200km of copper array cabling will connect the turbines to each other and two offshore sub-stations.  From there a further four export cables with a total length of 200km lead to a dedicated on-shore sub-station. 

We understand that the turbines used in this project are the traditional design using a gearbox and as such, they are not particularly copper intensive but even so, we estimate that around 2kt of copper will be used in the 175 turbines. However, this is dwarfed by our calculated use of copper in array cable between the turbines, subsea cable to shore and the two off-shore and one on-shore sub-stations, which according to our estimates comes to around 8.5kt.  In this case, it is the use of subsea cable that really ramps up copper consumption in this project and results in copper use outside of the turbines being over four times as much as is used in the turbines themselves.

## The weather forecast 

Combining data for wind capacity installations with estimates for copper used within turbines, we are able to estimate copper use in wind power.  Although for the purposes of this _Insight_ , we have used the year of installation as the year of copper consumption, copper will clearly have been consumed prior to that in the construction of turbines but given the availability of data, we feel that this is still a reasonable proxy.  We estimate that in Western Europe* there were 10GW of wind power installations in 2011, and that the use of copper within those turbines amounted to some 37kt tonnes. 

However, as we noted above, copper consumption arising from the installation of wind farms is not restricted to copper within the turbines as there is a requirement for related infrastructure.  This is much harder to quantify but could well be as much as is used in the turbines themselves, resulting in an estimated total copper consumption of 74kt in Western Europe last year.  As we noted above though, this is based on the premise that all copper was consumed within the year of installation. 

After a contraction in 2012 amid changes to incentive schemes in some countries, we forecast growth of 12% per year in wind capacity installations in Western Europe over the period 2013-2015.  We forecast that sectoral copper demand will actually run ah

ead of this pace because of the increasing prevalence of direct drive or gearless technology which uses more copper per MW. This is implicit within our forecasts because we expect off-shore wind installations to grow ahead of those on-shore and as a result, gearless technology which requires less maintenance is likely to be favoured. Meanwhile, the increasing penetration of off-shore wind turbines will boost the requirement for copper from related infrastructure and cable, providing a further lift to demand. ### **Western European* copper consumption in wind turbines – (kt)** 40 60

Relative to overall demand, copper consumed in turbines is still relatively small, accounting for less than 2% of total European demand. Compared to the electrical sector that it falls within, it still represents only around 5% at present. However, set against our forecast long term average annual growth in consumption of under 1% in Europe this is at least a growth story for copper.
